slides.heading: Electricity that behaves like a magnet
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a wire carrying current is surrounded by a magnetic field. Coils of wire make electromagnets, and a magnet can push on a wire that carries current.

visual.alt: Table of devices that use the magnetic effect of an electric current

slides.narration: Namaste! In this part we discover that an electric current behaves like a magnet. A wire carrying current pushes a compass needle aside. Wind the wire into a coil and you get an electromagnet that you can switch on and off. Put a current-carrying wire near a magnet and it is pushed, which is how every electric motor turns.

slides.heading: Oersted’s experiment
slides.body_md: In 1820 **Hans Christian Oersted** placed a compass needle just below a wire stretched along the north–south line. With **no current**, the needle pointed north along the wire. When a **current flowed**, the needle was **deflected**; reversing the current reversed the deflection. **Conclusion:** an electric current produces a **magnetic field** around it.

slides.narration: Over two hundred years ago, Oersted noticed something surprising. A compass needle lying under a wire turned away from north as soon as a current flowed in the wire. When he reversed the current, the needle turned the other way. He concluded that an electric current produces a magnetic field around it. This linked electricity and magnetism for the first time.

slides.heading: Field of a straight wire; the right-hand thumb rule
slides.body_md: The field lines round a long straight wire are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to it. The field is **stronger close to the wire** and **stronger for a larger current**. **Right-hand thumb rule:** hold the wire in the right hand with the **thumb along the current**; the **curled fingers** show the **direction of the field lines**.

slides.narration: Around a straight wire the field lines are circles with the wire at their centre. They are close together near the wire, where the field is strong, and spread out farther away. To find their direction, grip the wire in your right hand with your thumb along the current. Your fingers curl the way the field lines go.

slides.heading: Field of a circular loop
slides.body_md: Bend the wire into a **circular loop**. Near each part of the wire the lines are still small circles, but towards the **centre** they become **almost straight** and point **along the axis** of the loop. All the field lines inside the loop point the same way, so the loop behaves like a **thin flat magnet**: one face is a **north** pole and the other a **south** pole. More turns or more current give a stronger field at the centre.

slides.narration: When the wire is bent into a loop, the circles round each part of the wire all point the same way inside the loop. Near the centre they join up into almost straight lines along the axis. So a current loop acts like a flat magnet, with a north face and a south face. More current, or more turns, make it stronger.

slides.heading: The solenoid
slides.body_md: A **solenoid** is a long coil of many turns of insulated wire. Its field is like that of a **bar magnet**: inside, the lines are **straight and parallel** (a nearly uniform field); outside, they loop from one end to the other. **Polarity (clock rule):** look at an end — if the current there flows **anticlockwise**, that end is a **north** pole; **clockwise** — a **south** pole.

slides.narration: A solenoid is a long coil with many turns. Its field looks just like a bar magnet’s field. Inside the coil the lines are straight and evenly spaced. Outside, they loop round from one end to the other. To name the poles, look at one end. If the current there goes anticlockwise, that end is a north pole. If it goes clockwise, it is a south pole.

slides.heading: Worked example: which electromagnet is stronger?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two coils are wound on identical soft iron cores. Coil P has 200 turns and carries 1.5 A; coil Q has 500 turns and carries 0.5 A. The strength of each electromagnet increases with both the number of turns and the current. Compare them using N × I.

**P:** $N \times I = 200 \times 1.5 = 300$.

**Q:** $N \times I = 500 \times 0.5 = 250$.

**Answer:** P is the stronger electromagnet, although Q has more turns.

visual.alt: Table comparing turns, current and their product for two electromagnets

slides.narration: Both the number of turns and the current make an electromagnet stronger, so we compare turns times current. Coil P has two hundred turns carrying one and a half amperes, giving three hundred. Coil Q has five hundred turns but only half an ampere, giving two hundred and fifty. So P is stronger, even though Q has more turns.

slides.heading: Electromagnets and permanent magnets
slides.body_md: An **electromagnet** is a solenoid wound on a **soft iron core**. Soft iron is **strongly magnetised** while current flows and **loses almost all its magnetism** when the current stops. **To make it stronger:** increase the **number of turns**, increase the **current**, use a **soft iron core** (a U-shaped core brings the poles close together). **Uses:** electric bell, cranes that lift scrap iron, relays, separating iron from waste, loudspeakers and motors.

rows: Can be changed with current or turns

visual.alt: Table comparing an electromagnet with a permanent magnet

slides.narration: An electromagnet is a coil wound on soft iron. Soft iron becomes a strong magnet while current flows and loses its magnetism as soon as the current stops. To make it stronger, add more turns, increase the current or use a soft iron core. Unlike a permanent magnet, it can be switched off, its strength can be changed, and its poles can be reversed.

slides.heading: An electromagnet at work
slides.body_md: With the key **closed**, current in the coil magnetises the soft iron core and it **attracts iron pins**. When the key is **opened**, the core is **demagnetised** and the pins **drop**. A **steel** core would keep some magnetism, so the pins would not fall — which is why electromagnets use **soft iron**.

slides.heading: Force on a conductor; Fleming’s left-hand rule
slides.body_md: A conductor carrying a current in a magnetic field experiences a **force**. The force is **greatest** when the conductor is **at right angles** to the field and **zero** when it lies **along** the field. Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force. **Fleming’s left-hand rule:** stretch the **thumb, forefinger and middle finger** of the **left hand** at right angles. **Forefinger → field, middle finger → current, thumb → force (motion).**

slides.narration: A wire carrying current between the poles of a magnet is pushed sideways. The push is strongest when the wire is at right angles to the field, and there is no push when the wire lies along the field. To find the direction, use your left hand. Forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current, and your thumb shows the force.

slides.heading: Worked example: using the left-hand rule
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A horizontal wire runs from west to east and carries a current towards the east. A magnetic field acts vertically **downwards** on it. Find the direction of the force on the wire.

**Step 1.** Forefinger (field): point it **down**.

**Step 2.** Middle finger (current): point it **east**.

**Step 3.** Thumb (force): it points **north**.

**Answer:** the wire is pushed **towards the north**, horizontally.

visual.alt: Table applying Fleming’s left-hand rule to a wire carrying current east in a downward field

slides.narration: Set your left hand step by step. Point your forefinger down, along the field. Turn your hand so the middle finger points east, along the current. Your thumb now points north. So the wire is pushed towards the north. Practise this with your own hand, keeping all three fingers at right angles.

slides.heading: The DC motor: parts and energy
slides.body_md: A **DC motor** converts **electrical energy into mechanical (kinetic) energy**. Its main parts: a strong **field magnet** (N and S poles); a rectangular **coil (armature)** ABCD of many turns on a soft iron core, free to turn on an **axle**; a **split ring commutator** joined to the ends of the coil; two **carbon brushes** pressing on the split rings and joined to the **battery**. Motors are used in fans, mixers, washing machines and electric vehicles.

slides.narration: In the first part, a current made a magnetic field. Now we turn the idea round. A changing magnetic field can make a current flow in a coil. This is called electromagnetic induction. It is how power stations generate electricity and how transformers change the voltage before it reaches your home.

slides.heading: Electromagnetic induction
slides.body_md: Connect a coil to a **galvanometer**. **Push a magnet into the coil:** the needle deflects. **Hold it still:** no deflection. **Pull it out:** the needle deflects the **other way**. A current is induced **only while the magnetic field linked with the coil is changing**. Moving the coil instead of the magnet has the same effect. This is **electromagnetic induction**; the current is an **induced current**.

Pull the magnet out and the needle moves the other way. A current flows only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing. This effect is called electromagnetic induction.

slides.heading: What makes the induced current larger?
slides.body_md: The induced current is **larger** when: (1) the magnet or coil moves **faster**; (2) the coil has **more turns**; (3) a **stronger magnet** is used; (4) the coil has a **soft iron core**. It is **reversed** when the motion is reversed or the other pole is used. There is **no** induced current without **relative motion** (or another change in the field).

visual.alt: Table of changes and their effect on the induced current

slides.narration: You can increase the induced current in four ways. Move the magnet faster, use a coil with more turns, use a stronger magnet, or put soft iron inside the coil. Reversing the motion, or using the other pole, reverses the current. And if nothing moves and nothing changes, there is no induced current at all.

slides.heading: Fleming’s right-hand rule
slides.body_md: When a **straight conductor moves across a magnetic field**, a current is induced in it (if the circuit is complete). **Fleming’s right-hand rule:** stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the **right hand** at right angles. **Thumb → motion, forefinger → field, middle finger → induced current.** Use the **right** hand for **generators** (induced current) and the **left** hand for **motors** (force).

Point your thumb along the motion and your forefinger along the field. Your middle finger then gives the induced current. Remember, the right hand is for generators, and the left hand is for motors.

slides.heading: Worked example: direction of an induced current
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A straight wire lies between a north pole on the left and a south pole on the right. It is pushed **downwards** across the field. Find the direction of the induced current.

**Step 1.** Field (forefinger): from N to S, that is **to the right**.

**Step 2.** Motion (thumb): **downwards**.

**Step 3.** Induced current (middle finger): **out of the page**, towards you.

**Check:** pushing the wire **up** instead gives a current **into** the page, as in the figure.

visual.alt: Table applying Fleming’s right-hand rule to a wire pushed down between the poles

slides.narration: Set your right hand step by step. Forefinger to the right, from north to south. Thumb pointing down, along the motion. Your middle finger now points towards you, out of the page, so that is the direction of the induced current. If the wire is pushed up instead, everything reverses and the current flows into the page.

slides.body_md: An **AC generator** converts **mechanical energy into electrical energy**. The output current is **alternating**.

Its main parts are a strong magnet, an armature coil turned on an axle by a turbine or an engine, two complete slip rings, one joined to each end of the coil, and two carbon brushes that carry the current out to the circuit.

slides.heading: Household AC: frequency 50 Hz
slides.body_md: In **alternating current (AC)** the current keeps **reversing its direction**; in **direct current (DC)** it flows one way only (cells, batteries). The household supply in India is AC of **frequency 50 Hz**: **50 complete cycles every second**. One cycle takes $T = \dfrac{1}{f} = 0.02$ s (20 ms), and the direction reverses **twice in each cycle**.

visual.alt: Graph of household mains voltage against time over forty milliseconds. The voltage rises and falls smoothly like a wave, changing direction every ten milliseconds and completing one full cycle every twenty milliseconds, so there are fifty cycles each second.
visual.caption: One cycle takes 20 ms, so the frequency is 1 ÷ 0.02 s = 50 Hz.

slides.narration: The current from a cell flows one way only. This is direct current. The current from the mains keeps reversing direction. This is alternating current. In India it completes fifty cycles every second, so its frequency is fifty hertz. Each cycle lasts twenty milliseconds, and the direction changes twice in every cycle.

slides.heading: Worked example: frequency and period
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Find the time for one cycle of the 50 Hz mains. (b) How many times does the current change direction in one second? (c) How many cycles are completed in 2 minutes?

**(a)** $T = \dfrac{1}{50} = 0.02$ s, that is 20 ms.

**(b)** Two reversals per cycle: $2 \times 50 = 100$ times.

**(c)** $50 \times 120 = 6000$ cycles.

visual.alt: Table of the frequency, period and number of reversals of household AC

slides.narration: The period is one divided by the frequency, so one divided by fifty gives two hundredths of a second, or twenty milliseconds. The current reverses twice in every cycle, so it changes direction a hundred times each second. In two minutes, which is one hundred and twenty seconds, the supply completes six thousand cycles.

slides.heading: Quick check: household AC
slides.body_md: Relate the period and the frequency of the mains.
slides.narration: Quick check. Frequency is one divided by the time for one cycle.

slides.heading: Advantages of AC over DC
slides.body_md: **Advantages of AC:** (1) its voltage can be **stepped up or down easily with transformers**, so power can be sent at a very high voltage and a small current, with **little loss** in the lines; (2) AC generators are **simpler and cheaper** to build for large power; (3) AC can easily be **converted into DC** (rectified) when needed. **DC** is still needed for **charging batteries**, **electroplating** and electronic circuits.

rows: Reverses (50 times each way per second)

visual.alt: Table comparing alternating and direct current

slides.narration: Why is the mains supply alternating? The main reason is that alternating current can be stepped up or down easily with a transformer. Power can be sent at a very high voltage with a small current, so little energy is lost in the wires. Direct current is still needed for charging batteries and for electroplating.

slides.heading: The transformer
slides.body_md: A **transformer** changes an **alternating voltage**. It has a **primary coil** (connected to the AC input) and a **secondary coil** (giving the output), wound on a **laminated soft iron core**. The voltages are in the ratio of the turns: $\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$. **Step-up:** $N_{s} > N_{p}$, so $V_{s} > V_{p}$. **Step-down:** $N_{s} < N_{p}$, so $V_{s} < V_{p}$. A transformer **does not work on steady DC**.

slides.narration: A transformer has two coils on a soft iron core. The primary coil takes in alternating current, and the secondary coil gives out a different voltage. If the secondary has more turns, the voltage goes up, and it is a step-up transformer. If it has fewer turns, the voltage goes down, and it is a step-down transformer. It does not work with steady direct current.

slides.heading: Worked example: transformer voltages
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A step-down transformer in a doorbell has 2200 turns on its primary and 80 turns on its secondary. Find the output voltage from the 220 V mains. (b) A step-up transformer raises 220 V to 4400 V. Its primary has 150 turns. How many turns are on the secondary?

**(a)** $V_{s} = V_{p} \times \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = 220 \times \dfrac{80}{2200} = 8$ V.

**(b)** $N_{s} = N_{p} \times \dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = 150 \times \dfrac{4400}{220} = 3000$ turns.

visual.alt: Table of turns and voltages for the two transformers in the example

slides.narration: Use the turns ratio. For the doorbell transformer, the secondary has eighty turns out of two thousand two hundred, so the output is two hundred and twenty times eighty divided by two thousand two hundred, which is eight volts. For the step-up transformer, the voltage rises twenty times, so the secondary needs twenty times as many turns: three thousand.

notes.title: Electromagnetism — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Magnetic field of a current
sections.body_md:
- **Oersted’s experiment:** a compass needle below a north–south wire is deflected when a current flows; the deflection reverses with the current. A current produces a magnetic field.
- **Straight wire:** field lines are concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire; closer together (stronger field) near the wire and for a larger current.
- **Right-hand thumb rule:** grip the wire in the right hand with the thumb along the current; the fingers curl in the direction of the field.
- **Circular loop:** circles round each part of the wire; near the centre the lines are nearly straight along the axis. One face acts as N, the other as S. More turns or more current give a stronger field.

key_terms.definition_md: If a current-carrying wire is held in the right hand with the thumb along the current, the curled fingers point along the magnetic field lines.
A line along which a free north pole would tend to move; its tangent gives the field direction at a point.

visual.alt: Table of field-line shapes for three current-carrying conductors

sections.heading: 2. Solenoid and electromagnet
sections.body_md:
- **Solenoid:** a long coil of insulated wire; its field is like a bar magnet’s: straight and parallel inside, looping from N to S outside.
- **Clock rule:** viewed from one end, anticlockwise current — that end is N; clockwise — S. Reversing the current reverses the poles.
- **Electromagnet:** a solenoid on a soft iron core; a temporary magnet while current flows.
- **Stronger electromagnet:** more turns, more current, soft iron core (U-shaped to bring the poles close).
- **Soft iron, not steel:** soft iron is magnetised strongly and loses its magnetism when the current stops; steel keeps some magnetism.
- **Uses:** electric bell, cranes for scrap iron, relays, sorting iron from waste, loudspeakers, motors.

key_terms.definition_md: A long cylindrical coil of many turns of insulated wire whose magnetic field, when a current flows, resembles that of a bar magnet.
A temporary magnet made by passing a current through a coil wound on a soft iron core.

visual.alt: Table comparing an electromagnet and a permanent magnet

sections.heading: 3. Force on a conductor; DC motor
sections.body_md:
- A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a **force**: greatest when it is perpendicular to the field, zero when parallel; reversing the current or the field reverses the force.
- **Fleming’s left-hand rule:** thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular — forefinger: **field**, middle finger: **current**, thumb: **force (motion)**.
- **DC motor** (parts and energy only): field magnet; armature coil on an axle; **split ring commutator**; **carbon brushes**; DC source. Energy: **electrical → mechanical**.
- Uses: fans, mixers, washing machines, pumps, electric vehicles.

key_terms.definition_md: With the left hand’s thumb, forefinger and middle finger at right angles, forefinger along the field and middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of the force.
The split ring joined to the ends of the coil of a DC motor, on which the carbon brushes press.

rows: Coil that turns on an axle
Commutator joined to the coil ends

visual.alt: Table of the main parts of a DC motor

sections.heading: 4. Electromagnetic induction; AC generator; household AC
sections.body_md:
- **Electromagnetic induction:** a current is induced in a closed coil whenever the magnetic field linked with it **changes** (magnet or coil moving, or a nearby current changing). No change, no induced current.
- Larger induced current: faster motion, more turns, stronger magnet, soft iron core. Reversed motion or pole reverses it.
- **Fleming’s right-hand rule:** thumb — **motion**, forefinger — **field**, middle finger — **induced current**.
- **AC generator** (parts and energy only): field magnet; armature coil turned on an axle; **two slip rings**; carbon brushes; external circuit. Energy: **mechanical → electrical**.
- **Household AC in India: 50 Hz**; period $T = 1/f = 0.02$ s; the direction reverses twice per cycle.

key_terms.definition_md: The production of an electric current in a closed circuit by changing the magnetic field linked with it.
The number of complete cycles of an alternating current in one second, measured in hertz.

visual.alt: Table comparing the DC motor and the AC generator

sections.heading: 5. AC versus DC; transformers
sections.body_md:
- **AC advantages:** voltage easily changed by transformers (high-voltage, low-current transmission with little loss); generators simpler for large power; easily converted to DC. **DC** needed for charging batteries and electroplating.
- **Transformer:** primary and secondary coils on a **laminated soft iron core**; works **only on AC**.
- $\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$. **Step-up:** $N_{s} > N_{p}$ (power stations). **Step-down:** $N_{s} < N_{p}$ (chargers, doorbells, the pole transformer).
- For an ideal transformer, power in = power out: $V_{p}I_{p} = V_{s}I_{s}$, so stepping the voltage up steps the current down.

key_terms.definition_md: A transformer with more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary, so that the output voltage is greater than the input voltage.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary, so that the output voltage is less than the input voltage.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using the left hand for the field of a wire, or the right hand for the force on a wire.
- Saying a current is induced by a magnet at rest inside a coil.
- Mixing up split rings (motor) and slip rings (generator).
- Saying a transformer works on DC, or that a step-up transformer increases the current too.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Rules: the hand, what each finger represents, and that they are at right angles.
- Field diagrams: correct shape, arrows, spacing.
- Transformer sums: the ratio, substitution, answer with unit, and the type (step-up or step-down).

cards.front_md: When is the force on a current-carrying wire zero?
cards.back_md: When the wire lies along the field.

cards.front_md: Fleming’s left-hand rule: forefinger?
cards.back_md: Field.

cards.front_md: Fleming’s left-hand rule: thumb?
cards.back_md: Force (motion).

cards.front_md: Energy change in a DC motor?
cards.back_md: Electrical → mechanical.

cards.front_md: Parts of a DC motor?
cards.back_md: Field magnet, armature coil, split ring commutator, carbon brushes.

cards.front_md: Electromagnetic induction?
cards.back_md: A current induced in a coil by a changing magnetic field.

cards.front_md: Magnet at rest inside a coil: induced current?
cards.back_md: None.

cards.front_md: Two ways to increase an induced current?
cards.back_md: Move faster; use more turns (or a stronger magnet).

cards.front_md: Fleming’s right-hand rule: middle finger?
cards.back_md: Induced current.

cards.front_md: Energy change in an AC generator?
cards.back_md: Mechanical → electrical.

cards.front_md: Rings of an AC generator?
cards.back_md: Two slip rings (full rings).

cards.front_md: Frequency of household AC in India?
cards.back_md: 50 Hz.

cards.front_md: Period of 50 Hz AC?
Main advantage of AC over DC?
cards.back_md: Its voltage can be changed easily by transformers.

cards.front_md: Turns ratio of a transformer?
cards.back_md: Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np.

cards.front_md: Step-up transformer?
cards.back_md: More turns on the secondary; raises the voltage.

cards.front_md: Why does a transformer not work on DC?

cards.front_md: Exam tip: which hand?
cards.back_md: Left for motors (force), right for generators (induced current).

questions.stem_md: A long straight wire lies flat on this page and carries a current from the bottom of the page towards the top. At a point just to the right of the wire, the magnetic field is directed:

options.text_md: towards the top of the page
to the right, away from the wire

questions.solution_md: Right hand: thumb up the page; the fingers curl into the page on the right of the wire — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In Oersted’s experiment, a compass needle lying under a wire swung away from north when a current was switched on. This showed that:

options.text_md: a magnet produces an electric current in a wire
the wire had become a permanent magnet
the Earth’s magnetic field had reversed
an electric current produces a magnetic field around it

questions.solution_md: The current’s own magnetic field deflected the needle — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Iron filings are sprinkled on a card through which a long straight wire passes vertically, carrying a large current. The pattern shows:

options.text_md: straight lines radiating outwards from the wire
concentric circles that are farther apart at greater distances from the wire
circles that are equally spaced at all distances

questions.solution_md: The field lines are circles round the wire, and the field weakens with distance — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A long vertical wire passes through a horizontal card and carries a current upwards. A small compass on the card, due east of the wire, has its north pole pointing north (the field of the wire is much stronger than the Earth’s). The current is now reversed and the compass is moved to a point due west of the wire. Its north pole now points:
questions.solution_md: Upward current: the field is anticlockwise seen from above, so east of the wire it points north. Reversing the current makes the field clockwise, and west of the wire a clockwise field also points north. Both changes cancel — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reversing the current in a straight wire reverses the direction of the magnetic field around it.

**Reason (R):** By the right-hand thumb rule, the curl of the fingers gives the field direction when the thumb points along the current.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true; reversing the thumb reverses the curl of the fingers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Near the centre of a circular loop carrying a current, the magnetic field lines are nearly straight.
questions.solution_md: True: the circles round each part of the loop merge into nearly straight lines along the axis at the centre.

questions.stem_md: The deflection of a compass needle by a current in a nearby wire was first observed by ___.
The direction of the magnetic field round a straight current-carrying wire is given by the right-hand ___ rule.
questions.solution_md: Right-hand **thumb** rule.

questions.stem_md: State the right-hand thumb rule.

answer.model_answer_md: Grip the straight conductor in the right hand with the thumb pointing along the current: the direction in which the fingers curl is the direction of the magnetic field lines.

questions.solution_md: Thumb along current; fingers give field.

questions.stem_md: What conclusion did Oersted draw when a compass needle near a wire was deflected by a current?

answer.model_answer_md: That a current-carrying conductor sets up a magnetic field around itself.

questions.solution_md: Current produces a magnetic field.

questions.stem_md: State the clock rule for finding the polarity of an end of a solenoid.

answer.model_answer_md: Look at the end: if the current there flows clockwise the end is a south pole, and if anticlockwise it is a north pole.

questions.solution_md: Clockwise S, anticlockwise N.

questions.stem_md: A student places a small compass at different distances from a long straight wire carrying a steady current and records how far the needle swings from its starting position. At 2 cm the swing is 40°, at 4 cm it is 22° and at 8 cm it is 11°. (a) What do the readings show about the magnetic field as the distance from the wire increases? (b) The student wants the swing at 8 cm to be about 22°. What should be changed in the circuit, and why will it work?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The field gets weaker as the distance increases: the swing falls steadily, to roughly half each time the distance is doubled. (b) Increase the current in the wire. A larger current gives a stronger field at every distance, so the needle at 8 cm will swing farther.

questions.solution_md: Weaker with distance; more current.

questions.stem_md: A circular coil hangs in a vertical plane and carries a current. (a) Describe the field lines near the centre of the coil. (b) Seen from one face, the current flows anticlockwise. Which magnetic pole does that face behave as?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Near the centre they are almost straight and parallel, along the axis of the coil, at right angles to its plane. (b) A north pole.

questions.solution_md: Straight along the axis; north.

questions.stem_md: A student winds a coil on an iron nail and counts the paper clips it lifts. With 20 turns and 1.0 A it lifts 4 clips; with 40 turns and 1.0 A it lifts 8 clips; with 20 turns and 2.0 A it lifts 8 clips. Using the pattern in these readings, the number of clips lifted with 40 turns and 2.0 A would be about:
questions.solution_md: Doubling the turns doubles the strength (4 to 8) and doubling the current doubles it as well (4 to 8). Doing both doubles it twice: 4 × 2 × 2 = 16 — option (b). Adding the two gains (12) ignores that the effects multiply.

questions.stem_md: In an electric bell, the electromagnet pulls an iron armature, which makes the hammer strike the gong and also breaks the circuit so that a spring can pull the armature back. If the soft iron core were replaced by a steel rod of the same size, the bell would most likely:

options.text_md: ring once and then stick, because the steel stays magnetised and keeps holding the armature
ring continuously, but more loudly, because steel makes a stronger magnet
not ring at all, because steel cannot be magnetised
ring continuously, because steel conducts current better than iron

questions.solution_md: The bell works only if the core loses its magnetism as soon as the circuit breaks. A steel core stays magnetised, so the armature stays pulled in — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An electromagnet is holding a cluster of iron pins. The key in its circuit is opened. The pins fall because:

options.text_md: the pins become magnetised with the opposite polarity
the coil becomes a permanent magnet
the soft iron core loses its magnetism when the current stops
the Earth’s field becomes stronger than the core’s

questions.solution_md: No current, no magnetising field, and soft iron does not retain magnetism — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A shop’s fire door is held open against a spring by a magnet fixed in the wall. When the fire alarm trips, the door must close by itself. The wall magnet should be:

options.text_md: an electromagnet, switched off by the alarm so that it lets go of the door
a permanent magnet, because it never loses its strength
a permanent magnet, because the alarm can reverse its poles
an electromagnet with a steel core, which keeps holding the door after the current stops

questions.solution_md: Only an electromagnet with a soft iron core can be switched off to release the door; a permanent magnet cannot, and a steel core would stay magnetised — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Seen from its left end, the current in the coil of an electromagnet flows anticlockwise. A small compass is placed just beyond that left end, on the axis. The north pole of the compass needle points:

options.text_md: at right angles to the axis
in no particular direction, because the core is soft iron

questions.solution_md: Clock rule: anticlockwise means the left end is a north pole, which repels the north pole of the needle — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A coil with a soft iron core makes a stronger magnet than the same coil, carrying the same current, without a core.

**Reason (R):** Soft iron is a good conductor of electricity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the core strengthens the magnet because soft iron is easily magnetised, not because it conducts electricity — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A permanent magnet can be switched off when it is not needed.
questions.solution_md: False: only an electromagnet can be switched off, by stopping its current.

questions.stem_md: The core of an electromagnet is made of ___ iron.
questions.solution_md: **Soft** iron.

questions.stem_md: Looking at the left end of a solenoid, Arjun sees the current flowing anticlockwise. He brings the south pole of a bar magnet towards that end. The magnet and the solenoid ___ each other.
questions.solution_md: Clock rule: anticlockwise makes the left end a north pole, and a south pole is attracted to it, so they **attract**.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between an electromagnet and a permanent magnet.

answer.model_answer_md: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows; a permanent magnet keeps its magnetism. The strength and polarity of an electromagnet can be changed by changing the current; those of a permanent magnet are fixed.

questions.solution_md: Two differences.

questions.stem_md: A junkyard uses an electromagnet hung from a crane to move scrap cars. (a) Name two ways to make it lift heavier loads. (b) Why is its core made of soft iron? (c) Why can it not be used to move scrap aluminium?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Increase the current in the coil; increase the number of turns. (b) Soft iron is strongly magnetised while the current flows and lets go of the load when the current is switched off. (c) Aluminium is not attracted by a magnet (it is not a magnetic material).

questions.solution_md: Current and turns; soft iron; aluminium non-magnetic.

questions.stem_md: The electric motor inside a table fan converts:
questions.solution_md: A motor uses a current to produce motion — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In Fleming’s left-hand rule, the forefinger points in the direction of the:
questions.solution_md: Forefinger — field, middle finger — current, thumb — force — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A vertical wire carries a current upwards. A uniform magnetic field acts horizontally towards the north. The force on the wire acts towards the:
questions.solution_md: Left hand: forefinger north, middle finger up; the thumb points west — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A horizontal rod lies east–west and carries a current from west to east in a uniform horizontal magnetic field pointing north. The rod is pushed upwards. If both the current and the field are now reversed together, the rod is pushed:

options.text_md: nowhere, because the force becomes zero

questions.solution_md: Left hand: forefinger north, middle finger east, so the thumb points up. Reversing only one of the two would reverse the force, but reversing both restores it: upwards again — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a simple DC motor, the parts that press on the split rings and connect the rotating coil to the battery are the:
questions.solution_md: The carbon brushes slide on the split rings — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A current-carrying wire lying along the magnetic field lines experiences the largest possible force.

**Reason (R):** The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is false: a wire along the field lines experiences no force. R is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A simple DC motor uses two slip rings to connect its coil to the battery.
questions.solution_md: False: a DC motor uses a split ring commutator; slip rings belong to an AC generator.

questions.stem_md: The coil that turns between the poles of the magnet in a DC motor is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: **Armature**.

questions.stem_md: In a DC motor, the ends of the coil are joined to a ___ ring commutator.
questions.solution_md: **Split** ring commutator.

questions.stem_md: Use Fleming’s left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a wire in each case. (a) Current due east, field vertically downwards. (b) Current due east, field vertically upwards.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Forefinger down, middle finger east: the thumb points north. (b) Reversing the field reverses the force: south.

questions.solution_md: North; south.

questions.stem_md: Name four main parts of a simple DC motor and state the energy conversion that takes place in it.

answer.model_answer_md: Field magnet (N and S poles), armature coil on an axle, split ring commutator, carbon brushes (and a DC source). It converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

questions.solution_md: Four parts; electrical to mechanical.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet is held still inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. It is then pulled out quickly, held still beside the coil, and finally pushed back in slowly. The galvanometer needle shows:

options.text_md: zero, a large swing one way, zero, then a small swing the same way
zero, a small swing one way, zero, then a large swing the opposite way
a steady deflection, a large swing, a steady deflection, then a small swing
zero, a large swing one way, zero, then a small swing the opposite way

questions.solution_md: No change of field means zero; pulling out fast gives a large swing; pushing in reverses the change, so the swing reverses, and slow motion makes it small — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A straight horizontal rod lying north–south is moved due east through a magnetic field that acts vertically downwards. The current induced in the rod flows towards the:
questions.solution_md: Right hand: thumb east (motion), forefinger down (field); the middle finger points north — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A bicycle dynamo lights the lamp of a cycle. In the dynamo the energy conversion is:
questions.solution_md: A generator (dynamo) converts the energy of motion into electrical energy — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a simple AC generator, the two ends of the armature coil are connected to:

options.text_md: the two halves of a split ring
the two poles of the magnet

questions.solution_md: Each end has its own full slip ring — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The mains supply in Kunal’s home completes one full cycle every 20 ms. Its frequency is:
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{0.02} = 50$ Hz — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Pushing the north pole of a magnet slowly into a coil makes the galvanometer needle swing to the right. The same pole is then pulled out of the coil more quickly. The needle swings:

options.text_md: to the right, by a larger amount
to the left, by a smaller amount
not at all, because the magnet is leaving the coil
to the left, by a larger amount

questions.solution_md: Pulling out reverses the change of field, so the swing reverses (left); the faster change makes it larger — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A current is induced in a closed coil when a bar magnet is moved towards it.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic field linked with the coil changes while the magnet moves.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the changing field is the cause of the induced current — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Moving a coil towards a stationary magnet induces a current in it, just as moving the magnet towards the coil does.
questions.solution_md: True: only relative motion matters.

questions.stem_md: The production of a current in a coil by changing the magnetic field linked with it is called electromagnetic ___.
questions.solution_md: Electromagnetic **induction**.

questions.stem_md: In an AC generator, the two ends of the coil are joined to two ___ rings.
questions.solution_md: **Slip** rings.

questions.stem_md: In some countries the mains supply has a frequency of 60 Hz. How long, in milliseconds, does the supply take to go through 15 complete cycles?
questions.solution_md: $T = \dfrac{1}{60}$ s, so 15 cycles take $15 \times \dfrac{1}{60} = 0.25$ s $= 250$ ms.

questions.stem_md: A lamp is connected to the 50 Hz mains for 3 minutes. How many times does the current in the lamp reverse its direction in this time?
questions.solution_md: $t = 180$ s, so cycles $= 50 \times 180 = 9000$. The current reverses twice in every cycle, so reversals $= 2 \times 9000 = 18000$.

questions.stem_md: A coil is joined to a galvanometer. Pushing the north pole of a bar magnet into the coil at a steady speed makes the needle swing to the right. Predict the swing, with a reason, when (a) the same north pole is pulled out again at the same speed, and (b) the south pole is pushed in at twice that speed.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The needle swings to the left by about the same amount: the field through the coil is now decreasing, so the induced current is reversed. (b) The needle swings to the left, because the opposite pole reverses the direction of the change, and by a larger amount, because the field changes faster.

questions.solution_md: Left, same size; left, larger.

questions.stem_md: Name the main parts of a simple AC generator and state the energy conversion in it.

answer.model_answer_md: Field magnet, armature coil turned on an axle, two slip rings and two carbon brushes (with the external circuit). It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

questions.solution_md: Parts; mechanical to electrical.

questions.stem_md: A straight wire lies between the poles of a magnet, north pole on the left and south pole on the right. (a) State Fleming’s right-hand rule. (b) Find the direction of the induced current when the wire is pushed downwards. (c) What happens to the current if the wire is moved parallel to the field lines?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) With the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand at right angles, the thumb along the motion and the forefinger along the field, the middle finger gives the induced current. (b) Field to the right, motion down: the current flows out of the page. (c) No current is induced, since the wire does not cut across the field.

questions.solution_md: Rule; out of the page; zero.

questions.stem_md: A transformer has 400 turns on its primary coil and 8000 turns on its secondary coil. It is a:
questions.solution_md: More turns on the secondary raise the voltage — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A transformer is connected by mistake to a 12 V car battery. After the switch is closed it gives no output, because:

options.text_md: the battery voltage is too low for any transformer
a steady current does not produce a changing magnetic field in the core
the core becomes a permanent magnet
the secondary coil is short-circuited by the battery

questions.solution_md: Induction needs a changing field; steady DC gives none — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two designs send the same electric power through the same long cable: design X at 11 kV and design Y at 440 V. Compared with design Y, design X wastes:

options.text_md: less energy as heat in the cable, because its current is larger
less energy as heat in the cable, because its current is smaller
more energy as heat in the cable, because a higher voltage heats the wire more
the same energy, because the power sent is the same

questions.solution_md: For the same power P = VI, the higher voltage means a much smaller current, and the heat produced in the cable depends on the current — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A transformer in a hostel has 1000 turns on its primary and 100 turns on its secondary, and its primary is joined to the 220 V mains. The secondary supplies a current of 5 A. Assuming no energy is lost, the current drawn from the mains is:
questions.solution_md: $V_{s} = 220 \times \dfrac{100}{1000} = 22$ V, so the output power is $22 \times 5 = 110$ W. The primary takes the same power: $I_{p} = \dfrac{110}{220} = 0.5$ A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A step-down transformer has fewer turns on its secondary coil than on its primary coil.

**Reason (R):** A step-down transformer raises both the voltage and the current.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true (Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np). R is false: it lowers the voltage, and the current is stepped up — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A step-up transformer increases both the voltage and the current.
questions.solution_md: False: when the voltage is stepped up, the current is stepped down (power in about equals power out).

questions.stem_md: The coil of a transformer that is connected to the AC supply is called the ___ coil.
questions.solution_md: **Primary** coil.

questions.stem_md: The transformer of a bedside lamp has 2200 turns on its primary and 240 turns on its secondary, and its primary is connected to the 220 V mains. A small lamp joined across the secondary draws a current of 0.5 A. Find the power delivered to the lamp, in watts.
questions.solution_md: $V_{s} = V_{p} \times \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}} = 220 \times \dfrac{240}{2200} = 24$ V, so $P = V_{s}I_{s} = 24 \times 0.5 = 12$ W.

questions.stem_md: An ideal step-up transformer in a microwave oven takes 5 A from the 220 V mains and delivers a current of 0.5 A at its output. Its primary has 150 turns. How many turns does its secondary have?
questions.solution_md: For an ideal transformer $V_{p}I_{p} = V_{s}I_{s}$, so $\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{I_{p}}{I_{s}} = \dfrac{5}{0.5} = 10$ and $N_{s} = N_{p} \times \dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = 150 \times 10 = 1500$.

questions.stem_md: An ideal transformer steps 220 V down to 11 V for a set of garden lights that draw 4 A. Assuming no energy is lost, find the current, in amperes, taken from the mains by the primary coil.
A transformer takes a current of 0.5 A from the 220 V mains. Its secondary delivers 4 A at 22 V to a set of lamps. Find the efficiency of the transformer, as a percentage.
questions.solution_md: Input power $= 220 \times 0.5 = 110$ W; output power $= 22 \times 4 = 88$ W. Efficiency $= \dfrac{88}{110} \times 100 = 80\%$.

questions.stem_md: What is the frequency of the AC mains supply in India, and how long does one cycle take?

answer.model_answer_md: It is 50 Hz, so each cycle lasts one-fiftieth of a second, 20 ms.

questions.stem_md: A power station sends 22 kW of electric power to a town through two long, thin cables. (a) Find the current in the cables if the power is sent at 220 V, and if it is sent at 22000 V. (b) Which way wastes less energy as heat in the cables, and why can only an alternating supply be changed to that voltage easily?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$: at 220 V, $I = \dfrac{22000}{220} = 100$ A; at 22000 V, $I = \dfrac{22000}{22000} = 1$ A. (b) Sending at 22000 V wastes far less energy, because its current is 100 times smaller and the heating of the cables depends on the current. A transformer, which works only on AC, can raise the voltage for transmission and lower it again for use.

questions.solution_md: 100 A and 1 A; high voltage, transformer needs AC.

questions.stem_md: A transformer for a toy train has 1100 turns on its primary and 30 turns on its secondary, and its primary is joined to the 220 V mains. (a) Is it a step-up or a step-down transformer? Give a reason. (b) Calculate the output voltage. (c) Why would it not work if joined to a 6 V battery instead?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Step-down: the secondary has fewer turns than the primary. (b) $V_{s} = 220 \times \dfrac{30}{1100} = 6$ V. (c) A battery gives steady DC, which sets up no changing magnetic field in the core, so no voltage is induced in the secondary.

questions.solution_md: Step-down; 6 V; needs AC.

questions.stem_md: Match each rule in Column A with what it is used to find in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Direction of the field round a straight wire
Polarity of an end of a solenoid
Direction of the force on a current in a field

questions.solution_md: Thumb rule → field round a wire; left-hand rule → force; right-hand rule → induced current; clock rule → solenoid polarity.

questions.stem_md: Match each device in Column A with the correct description in Column B.

match_right.text_md: A temporary magnet with a soft iron core

questions.solution_md: Motor → electrical to mechanical; generator → mechanical to electrical; step-up transformer → raises AC voltage; electromagnet → temporary magnet.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe Oersted’s experiment. What did it show? [3]

(b) A long straight wire passes vertically through a horizontal card and carries a current upwards. (i) Describe the pattern of field lines on the card. (ii) Seen from above, are the lines clockwise or anticlockwise? (iii) How does the pattern change if the current is increased? [3]

(c) A solenoid is connected to a battery. (i) Compare its field with that of a bar magnet. (ii) How would you find which end is the north pole? (iii) State two ways of making its field stronger. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A wire is stretched along the north–south line just above a compass needle. With no current the needle points north; when a current flows the needle is deflected, and reversing the current reverses the deflection. So an electric current produces a magnetic field around it.

(b) (i) Concentric circles centred on the wire, farther apart away from the wire. (ii) Anticlockwise (thumb pointing up, towards the viewer). (iii) The field becomes stronger: the lines are drawn closer together and extend farther.

(c) (i) Like a bar magnet: straight parallel lines inside, looping from one end to the other outside. (ii) Look at an end: if the current there flows anticlockwise, that end is north (clock rule), or use a compass. (iii) More turns; more current (or a soft iron core).

questions.solution_md: Oersted; straight-wire field; solenoid.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is an electromagnet? Why is its core made of soft iron rather than steel? [3]

(b) Give three differences between an electromagnet and a permanent magnet. [3]

(c) (i) Name two devices that use electromagnets. (ii) How can the polarity of an electromagnet be reversed? (iii) Coil P has 300 turns carrying 1 A and coil Q has 150 turns carrying 2.5 A, on identical cores. Using N × I as a measure of strength, which is stronger? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A temporary magnet made by passing a current through a coil wound on a soft iron core. Soft iron is strongly magnetised while the current flows and loses its magnetism when the current stops; steel would stay magnetised.

(b) An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows, a permanent magnet always; its strength can be changed, a permanent magnet’s is fixed; its polarity can be reversed, a permanent magnet’s cannot.

(c) (i) Electric bell; crane for lifting scrap iron (also relays, loudspeakers). (ii) Reverse the current in the coil. (iii) P: $300 \times 1 = 300$; Q: $150 \times 2.5 = 375$; so Q is stronger.

questions.solution_md: Definition; differences; uses and comparison.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Fleming’s left-hand rule. When is the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (i) greatest and (ii) zero? [3]

(b) A horizontal wire carries current due north in a uniform magnetic field. Find the direction of the force when the field is (i) vertically downwards, (ii) vertically upwards and (iii) due north. [3]

(c) (i) Name the four main parts of a simple DC motor. (ii) State its energy conversion. (iii) Name two household appliances that use one. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:

(a) Give two advantages of AC over DC. Why is DC still needed for some purposes? [3]

(b) (i) A transformer has 500 turns on its primary and 10000 turns on its secondary, with 220 V on the primary. Find the output voltage. (ii) A pole transformer steps 11000 V down to 220 V and has 5000 turns on its primary. How many turns are on its secondary? [3]

(c) (i) Why is power transmitted at a high voltage? (ii) Why does a transformer not work on DC? (iii) An ideal transformer takes 0.5 A from the 220 V mains and gives 11 V. Find the output current. (iv) Is this transformer step-up or step-down? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) AC voltage can be changed easily with transformers, allowing high-voltage transmission with little loss; AC generators are simpler for large power and AC is easily converted to DC. DC is needed for charging batteries and electroplating, which need current in one direction.

(b) (i) $V_{s} = 220 \times \dfrac{10000}{500} = 4400$ V. (ii) $N_{s} = 5000 \times \dfrac{220}{11000} = 100$ turns.

(c) (i) For the same power, a high voltage means a small current, so less energy is lost as heat in the lines. (ii) A steady current gives no changing magnetic field, so nothing is induced in the secondary. (iii) $I_{s} = \dfrac{220 \times 0.5}{11} = 10$ A. (iv) Step-down.
